newsitem.title: UK: British unions less political under Labour - leader.
newsitem.headline: British unions less political under Labour - leader.

text.p: Britain's trade unions, which wielded enormous power in the 1960s and 1970s, will be much less political under a future Labour government, a top union leader said on Thursday.

John Edmonds, general secretary of the GMB general union, told Reuters that unions such as his would concentrate on workplace issues of direct relevance to their members rather than trying to influence political decisions.
Britain's unions wanted fairness, not favours, from a Labour government.

"I think we will be much less political than we were in the 1970s and much less political than the Australians have been." he said, referring to the 13-year Accord between Australian unions and a Labor government, which ended when Labor was ousted by a Liberal-National coalition last year.
Britain's opposition Labour party is widely expected to defeat the ruling Conservatives in an election due by May 22.

Labour leader Tony Blair has reduced the influence of trade unions on party policy as part of his efforts to shift Labour to the political centre, although unions such as the GMB are still major contributors to party funds.
But the ruling Conservatives still accuse Labour of being the tool of the trade unions.
Edmonds made it clear he had no wish to return to the days when top union leaders were entertained to "beer and sandwiches" by Labour prime ministers at 10, Downing Street.

He believed Australian trade unions would probably admit now that they had become too political during their period of cooperation with the government, neglecting their main function and losing members as a result.
"They neglected their industrial purpose to an extraordinary degree," Edmonds said.
"They became a very important element in the corporate state but a less important element in the workplace. If I have amything to do with it, we will not make that mistake."

"History tells us that governments don't give free lunches either," Edmonds said. "Anyone who looks at the history of the 1970s or at recent Australian history -- trade unions got no favours for which they didn't pay seven times over."
Unions looked forward to a less hostile climate under a Labour governmentbut a sympathetic administration could be only "30 to 40 percent" of the solution of some key problems.
"We have got to do the rest of the work ourselves," Edmonds added. "We are trade unionists first."
Unions hoped to work with a Labour government in key areas such as introducing a minimum wage, job creation and improving training.
They were also interested in issues such as investment, competition policy, regulating public utilities and the quality of public services.
"But they are all subsidiary to our activities in the workplace," Edmonds said.
The GMB has more than 500,000 members and is one of Britain's top five biggest unions.
